units.title: Short vowels in CVC words
units.rule: Short vowel words are like a drum beat: consonant, vowel, consonant. Say each sound, then write it.

units.title: Digraphs sh, ch, th, wh, ck
units.rule: Two letters can team up to make one new sound: sh, ch, th, wh. At the end of a short word, /k/ is spelled ck.

units.title: Initial and final blends
units.rule: In a blend, you hear each letter sound: s-t-o-p. Say the sounds slowly and write them in order.

units.title: Double letters and trigraphs (ff, ll, ss, zz, tch, dge)
units.rule: After a short vowel in a short word, f, l, s and z often double. The sound /ch/ after a short vowel is tch, and /j/ is dge.

units.title: VCe (silent e) syllables
units.rule: The silent e at the end is a helper. It makes the vowel say its name: cap becomes cape.

units.title: Open syllables and long vowels (me, go, my, fly)
units.rule: When a word ends in a vowel, the vowel says its name: go, me, fly. The letter y can say long i or long e.

units.title: Vowel teams (ai/ay, ee/ea, oa/ow, oo)
units.rule: Sometimes two vowels walk together and one says its name: rain, tree, boat. Use ai and oa in the middle of a word, ay and ow at the end.

units.title: R-controlled vowels (ar, or, er, ir, ur)
units.rule: When r follows a vowel, it changes the sound. ar says /ar/, or says /or/, and er, ir, ur all say /er/.

units.title: Endings -s, -es, -ed, -ing
units.rule: Add -s to make more than one. Add -es after s, x, sh and ch. Add -ed for past time and -ing for doing it now. Double the last letter after a short vowel.

units.title: Compound words
units.rule: Two small words can join to make a bigger word. Spell each little word, then put them together.

units.title: High-frequency and sight words
units.rule: Some words do not follow the rules. Learn them by heart and spell them without sounding out.

units.title: Bee challenge words
units.rule: These are longer words for a spelling bee. Break them into syllables to spell them.

units.title: Long vowels: VCe and vowel-team review
units.rule: Long vowels can be spelled with a silent e (slide) or with a vowel team (train, float). Pick the pattern that fits the word you hear.

units.title: Diphthongs and variant vowels (oi/oy, ou/ow, aw/au, oo)
units.rule: Some vowel pairs glide: oi and oy say /oy/, ou and ow say /ow/, aw and au say /aw/. Use oi, ou and au in the middle, and oy, ow and aw at the end.

units.title: R-controlled vowels (ar, or, er, ir, ur, ear, air)
units.rule: A vowel followed by r makes a new sound. er, ir and ur sound the same, so you have to remember which one the word uses.

units.title: Silent letters (kn, wr, gn, mb)
units.rule: Some letters are quiet. The k in kn, the w in wr, the g in gn, and the b after m do not make a sound, but they are still there when we spell.

units.title: Soft c and soft g
units.rule: When c or g is followed by e, i or y, it often turns soft. c says /s/ like in city and g says /j/ like in giant.

units.title: Contractions
units.rule: A contraction squeezes two words into one. The apostrophe shows where letters are missing: do not becomes don't.

units.title: Compound words
units.rule: Join two whole words with no letters lost. Say each part, then write both parts together.

units.title: Endings -s/-es/-ies, -ed and -ing (drop e, double, y to i)
units.rule: Before adding -ed or -ing, check the base word. Drop a silent e (hope, hoping). Double the last letter after one short vowel (stop, stopped). Change y to i before -es or -ed (baby, babies).

units.title: Endings -er and -est (comparing)
units.rule: Add -er to compare two things and -est to compare three or more. Watch for double letters (big, bigger) and y to i (happy, happier).

units.title: Prefixes un-, re-, dis-
units.rule: A prefix goes at the front and changes the meaning. un- means not, re- means again, and dis- means the opposite. The base word keeps all its letters.

units.title: Two-syllable words: VCCV and double consonants
units.rule: Split a two-syllable word between two consonants: rab-bit, but-ter. If the middle letters are doubled, each syllable gets one. Clap each beat to check.

units.title: High-frequency and sight words
units.rule: These words do not play by the sound rules. Practice them until you can spell them without thinking.

units.title: Bee challenge words
units.rule: These tougher words have several syllables or tricky parts. Say each syllable out loud as you spell.

units.title: Closed syllables in longer words
units.rule: A closed syllable ends in a consonant, so the vowel is short: nap-kin, mag-net. Break the word into beats and spell each one.

units.title: Open syllables in longer words
units.rule: An open syllable ends in a vowel, so the vowel says its name: pa-per, mu-sic. Listen for the long vowel at the end of the first syllable.

units.title: VCe syllables in longer words
units.rule: A syllable with silent e still says its long vowel name: re-mote, ex-plode. Keep the silent e at the end of that syllable.

units.title: Vowel teams, digraphs and diphthongs in longer words
units.rule: Vowel teams stay together in one syllable: mail-box, af-ter-noon. Remember which team makes the sound, like ai, ea, oa, oo, oi, ou.

units.title: R-controlled syllables in longer words
units.rule: In an r-controlled syllable, the vowel and r stay together: gar-den, mon-ster. Remember ar, or, er, ir, ur.

units.title: Final stable syllables (consonant-le)
units.rule: Many words end with a consonant plus le: ta-ble, bub-ble. The last syllable is its own beat, and the vowel before it follows the rules.

units.title: Homophones, set 1
units.rule: Homophones sound alike but have different spellings and meanings. Use the meaning in the sentence to choose the right one.

units.title: Homophones, set 2
units.rule: More sound-alike words. Picture the meaning first, then pick the spelling that matches it.

units.title: Contractions
units.rule: A contraction joins two words and uses an apostrophe in place of the missing letters. Say the long form to find where the apostrophe goes.

units.title: Compound words
units.rule: Compound words are two words joined together. If you can spell each part, you can spell the whole word.

units.title: Syllable division (VCCV, VCV, VCCCV)
units.rule: VCCV: split between the two consonants (den-tist). VCV: try splitting before the consonant (lem-on vs. pi-lot). VCCCV: split after the first or second consonant (hun-dred).

units.title: Prefixes (pre-, mis-, non-, sub-, un-, re-)
units.rule: A prefix is added to the front of a word and changes its meaning. pre- means before, mis- means wrong, non- means not, sub- means under. Do not change the spelling of the base word.

units.title: Suffixes (-ful, -less, -ly, -ment, -ness)
units.rule: A suffix goes at the end. -ful means full of, -less means without, -ly tells how, -ment and -ness make nouns. Add the suffix to the whole base word.

units.title: Suffixes that change the base word (drop e, change y to i, double the consonant)
units.rule: Sometimes the base word changes when you add a suffix. Drop the silent e before -ing or -ed (dance, dancer). Change y to i before most endings (happy, happily). Double the last letter after one short vowel (swim, swimming).

units.title: High-frequency and sight words
units.rule: These words are used all the time in reading and writing. Some do not follow the rules, so memorize the tricky parts.

units.title: Bee challenge words
units.rule: Longer words for a spelling bee. Think about syllables, silent letters and tricky vowels.

units.title: Vowel teams and diphthongs in multisyllabic words
units.rule: Longer words often hide vowel teams like oa, ea, oi, ou, ew. Keep each team together inside its syllable.

units.title: Unusual spellings (ough, augh, eigh, ph, ch as /k/)
units.rule: Some sounds have odd spellings. ough and augh can say /aw/ or /o/, eigh says long a, ph says /f/, and ch can say /k/. Learn these words by sight.

units.title: Final syllables -tion, -sion, -ture
units.rule: Endings like -tion and -sion say /shun/ and -ture says /cher/. They are always the last syllable and are never stressed.

units.title: Homophones and commonly confused words
units.rule: Homophones sound the same but mean different things. Read the whole sentence to decide which spelling fits.

units.title: Advanced syllable division (V/V, VCV, VCCCV)
units.rule: When two vowel sounds sit side by side, split between them: qui-et, ra-di-o. For three consonants in a row, split after the first or second: con-struct.

units.title: Prefixes (inter-, over-, under-, super-, trans-, mid-, fore-)
units.rule: These prefixes change the meaning: inter- means between, over- means too much or above, under- means below, super- means above or great, trans- means across, mid- means middle.

units.title: Suffixes (-able, -ible, -ous, -ious)
units.rule: -able and -ible mean can be done. -ous means full of. If the base is a whole word, you usually use -able. If not, you often need -ible.

units.title: Base-word changes (drop e, double the consonant, y to i)
units.rule: When you add a suffix, check the base word. Drop e before -ing, -ed, -able. Double the last consonant if the word ends with one vowel and one consonant in a stressed syllable. Change y to i before most endings.

units.title: Latin roots (spect, port, dict, struct, rupt, aud, vis)
units.rule: Many English words come from Latin roots. spect means look, port means carry, dict means say, struct means build, rupt means break, aud means hear, vis means see.

units.title: Greek roots (tele, photo, graph, bio, geo, therm, micro, auto)
units.rule: Some words are built from Greek parts. tele means far, photo means light, graph means write, bio means life, geo means earth, therm means heat, micro means tiny, auto means self.

units.title: High-frequency and tricky words
units.rule: These words are common but easy to misspell. Look for the part that surprises you, like the silent letters in listen and island.

units.title: Bee challenge words
units.rule: These words are tough. Break them into syllables and watch for silent letters and double consonants.

units.title: Consonant changes: /t/ to /sh/ and /k/ to /sh/
units.rule: Some words change their consonant sound when you add an ending: select becomes selection (t to sh), and music becomes musician (k to sh). Spell the base word, then add -tion, -ssion or -cian.

units.title: Endings -cial, -tial, -cious, -tious
units.rule: The sounds /shul/ and /shus/ have two spellings each. Words like social and special use c, and words like essential and ambitious often use t. Learn each word by sight.

units.title: Endings -ance, -ence, -ant, -ent
units.rule: These endings sound almost the same, so you must remember which one the word uses. Look for patterns, but check the dictionary if you are not sure.

units.title: Prefixes in-, im-, il-, ir-, non-, anti-
units.rule: The prefix in- means not, but it changes to im- before b, m, p, il- before l, and ir- before r. Notice the double letter when the base starts with the same letter, like il-legal and ir-regular.

units.title: Prefixes sub-, trans-, semi-, bi-, tri-, multi-, co-, ex-
units.rule: Prefixes tell a number or direction: sub- is under, trans- is across, semi- is half, bi- is two, tri- is three, multi- is many, co- is together, ex- is out.

units.title: Suffixes with base-word changes (-ed, -ing, -able, -ment, -ness)
units.rule: Check the base before you add. Double the last consonant when the stress is on the last syllable (occur, occurred). Change y to i (identify, identified). Keep the silent e after soft c or g (notice, noticeable).

units.title: Latin roots (ject, mit/miss, scrib/script, tract, vert, form)
units.rule: ject means throw, mit and miss mean send, scrib and script mean write, tract means pull, vert means turn, form means shape. Knowing the root helps you spell and understand new words.

units.title: Greek roots and combining forms (hydr, astro, geo, -ology, meter)
units.rule: hydr means water, astro means star, -ology means the study of, meter means measure. Break these long words into their roots to spell them.

units.title: Commonly confused words and homophones
units.rule: These pairs sound alike or nearly alike. Learn a memory trick for each: affect is an action, effect is a result; stationary means still, stationery is paper.

units.title: Silent letters and borrowed words
units.rule: English borrows words from other languages and keeps odd spellings. Watch for silent letters (debt, column), ph and gh, and the ch that says /sh/ (chef).

units.title: Irregular plurals
units.rule: Most nouns add -s or -es. Some end in f and change to ves (wolf, wolves). Words ending in consonant plus o often take -es (potato, potatoes). Some change completely (tooth, teeth).

units.title: High-frequency and frequently misspelled words
units.rule: These words show up in writing all the time. Practice the tricky part of each one.

units.title: Bee challenge words
units.rule: Tough words for spelling bee champions. Use roots, syllables and word history to help.

units.title: Latin roots, set 1 (aqua, ann, bene, cred, dur, fract, lum, mar, mort, nov, ped)
units.rule: Roots carry meaning. aqua means water, ann means year, cred means believe, dur means last, lum means light, mar means sea, mort means death, nov means new, ped means foot. Break the word into root and ending to spell it.

units.title: Latin roots, set 2 (cede/ceed, clud/clos, flect, gen, grat, loc, mot, pel, sens, tens)
units.rule: cede and ceed mean go, clud and clos mean shut, flect means bend, gen means birth, grat means pleasing, loc means place, mot means move, pel means push, sens means feel. Only three words end in -ceed: proceed, exceed, succeed.

units.title: Greek roots, set 2 (arch, gram, log, morph, path, phil, scope, syn, chron, cycl)
units.rule: arch means chief, gram means written, log means word or study, morph means shape, path means feeling, phil means love, scope means see, syn means together, chron means time, cycl means circle.

units.title: Suffix families (-ity, -ive, -ize, -ify, -ism, -ist)
units.rule: Suffixes tell the part of speech. -ity makes a noun, -ive makes an adjective, -ize and -ify make verbs, -ism and -ist name a belief or a person. Watch how the base changes (create, creative; electric, electricity).

units.title: Commonly confused terms (TEKS 6.10D.ix)
units.rule: The state standards name its/it's, affect/effect, there/their/they're and to/two/too. Those are in grades 2 and 5, so review them here with more pairs. Think about what the sentence means before you choose.

units.title: Academic vocabulary
units.rule: These words appear in textbooks and tests. Use a dictionary to check the spelling, syllables and pronunciation.

units.title: Silent and unusual letters in advanced words
units.rule: These words keep letters that are no longer pronounced, like the p in pneumonia and the h in honest. Use the dictionary to check the pronunciation and origin of each one.

units.title: Advanced endings (-eous, -ious, -ible, -able)
units.rule: Adjectives often end in -ous (full of) or -ible and -able (can be done). Say each syllable clearly, then match the ending to the pattern: courteous, responsible, adorable.

units.title: Double consonants and tricky spellings
units.rule: Many hard words have double letters in unexpected places, like accommodate (two c's, two m's). Make up a memory trick and check the dictionary.

units.title: Same spelling, different stress (record, present, content)
units.rule: Some words are spelled the same but stressed differently as nouns and verbs: REcord (noun) vs. reCORD (verb). Use the dictionary for the syllables and pronunciation.

units.title: Word origins (borrowed words and Texas words)
units.rule: Many English words came from other languages. Spanish gave Texas rodeo, ranch and patio. Use a dictionary to look up where a word came from and how to spell it.

units.title: Frequently misspelled words
units.rule: These words are tricky for lots of writers. Make a memory trick for the hard part, and check a dictionary.

units.title: Bee challenge words
units.rule: Championship-level words. Listen to the definition, ask about the language of origin, say each syllable, then spell.
